clues.title: Landscape: very mountainous with fjords
text: Norway is a very mountainous country, with many fjords along most of the coast.
NOTE: Finland and Denmark are both mostly flat, while Sweden has a mixture of flat, hilly and mountainous areas.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Very mountainous, with fjords along most of the coast. Finland and Denmark are mostly flat, and Sweden is a mix of flat, hilly and mountainous.

clues.title: Houses: wooden, red or black, many white
text: The vast majority of Norwegian houses are made of **wood**. Many houses are painted **red**, which is also typical for Sweden and Finland. **Black** painted houses are also quite common, more so than in Sweden or Finland.

NOTE: While the architecture is very similar to that of Sweden and Finland, there are some small, general differences. Sweden and Finland generally have more red and yellow houses, while Norway generally has more white houses. There is also a larger percentage of wooden houses in suburbs and near town centres in Norway than in Sweden and Finland, which use more brick than Norway.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Nearly all houses are wooden. Many are red, and black ones are more common than in Sweden or Finland. Norway has more white houses and fewer brick or yellow ones.

differs.how: More red and yellow houses, more brick
More red and yellow houses, more brick

clues.title: Plate: long white, green for vans
text: Norway has long white licence plates with the standard European strip on the left.
Commercial plates are **green**. These are often seen on vans.
NOTE: Within Europe, green licence plates are most commonly seen in Norway, but can also be found on electric vehicles in several other countries.

images.caption: Norwegian plates: white standard and green commercial
Norwegian plates: white standard and green commercial

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Long white plates with the European strip on the left. Commercial vehicles, often vans, have green plates. In Europe green plates are most common here but also appear on electric vehicles elsewhere.

clues.title: Road lines: long dashed edges, yellow centre
text: Smaller Norwegian roads typically have **long dashed** white outer lines, while larger roads have solid outer lines and **yellow middle lines**. The yellow lines have a distinct tinge of orange.

NOTE: Sweden only has white road lines, and the [dashes](https://www.google.se/maps/@55.8603502,14.0645816,3a,67.7y,310.56h,67.2t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sxSuRl8lj2S2ldx_vzphffQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?shorturl=1) on outer lines are shorter than in Norway. [Finnish](https://www.google.com/maps/@?api=1&map_action=pano&pano=c8FOHjmvgdL7njxYf5Hb6Q&viewpoint=64.117952,26.646979&heading=97.5109375143503&pitch=-14.532690519627238&fov=56.68574773360253&shorturl=1#extra%5Btags%5D=road+lines) outer road lines are always solid, and middle lines can be yellow or white.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Small roads have long dashed white edge lines. Larger roads have solid edges and an orange-tinted yellow middle line. Sweden has shorter dashes and only white lines, Finland has solid edges.

differs.how: Edge dashes are shorter, only white lines
Solid edge lines, centre line yellow or white

clues.title: Road lines: made of small dots of paint
text: Road lines will often be made up of **small dots** of paint.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Road lines are often made of small dots of paint rather than smooth paint.

clues.title: Language: Æ, Ø and Å, "kk" spelling
text: The Norwegian language contains the special letters Æ, Ø and Å.
NOTE: The special letters found in Norwegian can also be found in some of the other Nordic languages:
- Danish uses Æ, Ø and Å.
- Swedish uses Å, but not Æ or Ø. Norwegian also uses more E’s than Swedish, while Swedish uses more A’s instead. Norwegian uses “kk” where Swedish uses “ck”.
- Icelandic uses Æ, but not Ø or Å.
- Finnish uses Å, although it is viewed as a Swedish letter.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Norwegian uses Æ, Ø and Å, the same as Danish. Swedish has Å but not Æ or Ø and spells with "ck" where Norwegian uses "kk".

differs.how: Has Å but no Æ or Ø, and spells "ck"

clues.title: Bollard: thin curved, black parallelogram
text: Norway uses thin, curved rectangular bollards with the reflector inside of a **black** parallelogram.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A thin, curved rectangular bollard with the reflector inside a black parallelogram.

clues.title: Snow pole: orange, thin white reflector mid-pole
text: Norwegian snow poles are typically orange, with a **fairly** **thin** white reflector. The reflector is normally toward the **middle** of the pole.

NOTE: [Swedish](https://www.google.se/maps/@61.9908262,14.5790953,3a,39.6y,258.06h,61.21t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s1qT_52M1QOthv1f9cvsoXw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) snow poles typically have a wider reflector slightly higher up, and [Finnish](https://www.google.com/maps/@60.4814738,23.2577925,3a,15y,68.45h,69.44t,0.35r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s7-wUFACQ9NzGxHQu6ngnUw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) snow poles have their reflector at the very top.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Orange snow poles with a fairly thin white reflector near the middle of the pole. Swedish ones have a wider reflector set higher up.

differs.how: Wider reflector set higher on the pole

clues.title: Snow pole: thin wooden with painted reflector
text: It is also fairly common to find thin **wooden** snow poles with painted reflectors.
NOTE: While wooden snow poles can be found in [other Nordic countries](https://goo.gl/maps/ebwqngpn358DdBpp9), they will typically not have reflectors.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Thin wooden snow poles with painted reflectors are fairly common. In other Nordic countries wooden ones usually have no reflector.

clues.title: Guardrail: wooden posts
text: Guardrails often have **wooden posts**.
NOTE: This is not common in Sweden or Finland.

images.caption: Wooden posts holding the guardrail; circle zooms in on a post

clues.summary: Guardrails often have wooden posts, which is uncommon in Sweden and Finland.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian crossing, four stripes
text: Norwegian pedestrian signs typically have **four stripes** and a very simply drawn person. Note however, that there is a version with [five stripes](https://www.google.com/maps/@69.6519241,18.9565431,3a,15y,247.79h,95.06t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sr44nQpcvP6QQiIoQ5x9iPg!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) and a version where the person is more detailed and [wearing a hat](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.9150958,10.7314409,3a,15y,221.76h,97.28t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sxUjNRfgz1D4jn2MrTFqN3A!2e0!7i16384!8i8192).

NOTE: While [Finnish](https://www.google.com/maps/@61.4993731,23.759534,3a,15y,50.36h,98.09t,359.73r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sklmrQCHLp2po9CQARyRyMA!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) pedestrian signs have five stripes, Swedish pedestrian signs have four stripes. However, the person on [Swedish](https://www.google.se/maps/@59.8459127,17.6306563,3a,15y,112.66h,95.96t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s-ODCYQW5xsTcVebPn08xRQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) signs is detailed, but without a hat.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A crossing sign with four stripes and a very simple drawn person. A five-stripe version and a version with a hat also exist. Finland has five stripes, Sweden four stripes but a more detailed person.

differs.how: Four stripes but a detailed person without a hat
Five stripes
Four stripes too, but not the bold simple person

clues.title: Direction sign: yellow with black border
text: Norwegian directional signs are **yellow** with a **black border**. You will commonly see the road number displayed, either in a green box for European highways and major roads, or in a white box, for smaller roads.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Direction signs are yellow with a black border. The road number sits in a green box for European and major roads, or a white box for smaller roads.

clues.title: Sign: blue sign with large white M
text: On smaller roads, it is common to see these blue signs with a **large white M**.

NOTE: Similar signs can be found in [Sweden](https://goo.gl/maps/DqYAkha51nY72ao49), however the font is distinctly different. The middle point of the M does not extend to the bottom of the letter. There are no similar signs in Finland.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Small roads often have blue signs with a large white M. Sweden has similar signs, but its M's middle point does not reach the bottom. Finland has none.

clues.title: Bus stop sign: small blue with a white bus
text: Norwegian bus stops usually have this small, **blue sign** with a white bus.
NOTE: Sweden has a lot of different bus stops, none of which look like this.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stops usually have a small blue sign with a white bus. Sweden has many bus stop styles but none like this.

clues.title: Speed sign: white sign saying "Sone"
text: **White signs** with the text “**Sone**”, generally featuring a speed limit, are common in urban areas.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: White signs that say "Sone", usually with a speed limit, are common in towns.

clues.title: Street sign: names ending in -vei or -gate
text: The most common street name suffixes in Norway are [**vei**](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.9593416,10.6791889,3a,15y,271.42h,95.43t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sCK4o9jIF2f-laJXC2Mr2-A!2e0!5s20220501T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) and [**gate**](https://www.google.com/maps/@60.3989197,5.3282393,3a,15y,61.21h,100.75t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sS3foVfd95KVJKP139aYT3w!2e0!5s20220901T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu). While attached to the name, they take the forms [-veien](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.9224766,10.7556273,3a,15y,112.61h,94.04t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sl5Rng63pEh4G3UgU4do21Q!2e0!5s20230801T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) and [-gata](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.9248979,10.7238512,3a,15y,63.13h,100.43t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1scDDP0zNgkLdGMTV8fFpsyg!2e0!5s20230401T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) or [-gate](https://www.google.com/maps/@58.9672287,5.7464844,3a,15y,147.13h,91.89t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sk4Il9mVs8YiuVelO7sXz4g!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu).
NOTE: Swedish street names use the suffixes väg or vägen and gata or gatan, where gata is always detached from the name. Danish uses vej and gade.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The most common street name endings are vei and gate, joined to the name as -veien or -gata.

clues.title: Street sign: centred on top of the post
text: Street signs will generally be **centred** on top of sign posts.
NOTE: Street signs in Sweden will normally be attached either to the side of [sign posts](https://goo.gl/maps/YnsWJyWT27GYkDXGA) or [lamp posts](https://goo.gl/maps/JyeS5LBN8nZDyKrt8).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Street name signs are mounted centred on top of sign posts. In Sweden they are fixed to the side of posts or lamp posts.

text: Norwegian traffic signs have a red outline and a **white background**.

clues.summary: Road construction signs have a bright yellow background.

clues.title: Sign: four bolts in a tall rectangle
text: Most smaller road signs will be attached with four visible **sign bolts** in the shape of a tall rectangle. Beware that you may occasionally find [framed signs](https://www.google.com/maps/@58.8495149,5.7367006,3a,21.3y,31.15h,97.95t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sXRj68ZaFOCOFubBo1k50Nw!2e0!5s20221001T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) instead, particularly in urban settings.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most small road signs are fixed with four visible bolts in a tall rectangle. Framed signs also appear sometimes, mostly in towns.

clues.title: Chevron: yellow on black
text: Norway uses **yellow on black** chevrons.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Curve chevrons are yellow arrows on black.

clues.title: Route marker: small white square sign
text: Small **white square signs**, displaying the road number on top, and the distance to the closest town, are common to see along medium sized roads.

The road number will be preceded either by an R or an [F](https://www.google.se/maps/@62.2252395,6.269883,3a,15y,195.25h,79.98t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sz50wFAvEtsVFmAutPi8UBQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192). F roads show up as Fv on the map and are generally difficult to locate, while R roads lack any letters on the map and are generally more findable.

images.caption: Red circle marks the small white km marker post beside the water

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Small white square signs showing the road number and the distance to the nearest town are common on medium roads. The number starts with R or F. F roads are hard to locate, R roads are easier.

text: Norwegian poles are normally **wooden** and often have a small black metal cap on the top.

NOTE: Sweden and Finland use [double bolting](https://maps.app.goo.gl/JHaTnCsGhkTjLMXJA).

clues.summary: Lamps on wooden poles are held by one thick bolting. Sweden and Finland use a double bolting.

text: Traditional houses in Norway commonly have **grass covered roofs**.
NOTE: This is far less common in Sweden and Finland.

clues.summary: Traditional houses often have grass-covered roofs, which is much less common in Sweden and Finland.

clues.title: Google car: low smallcam, wide round blur
text: Norway has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Northern Europe also has smallcam.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The newer Gen 4 smallcam sits lower than normal with a big round blur and a small bump at the front. It can be see-through. Most of Northern Europe has it.

clues.title: Route marker: first digit shows the region
text: The first digit of Norwegian road numbers are region dependent. Note that there are some exceptions among single and two-digit roads.

There are also a small number of roads beginning with a 9: [Road 9](https://www.google.com/maps/@59.1490125,7.5378803,3a,90y,335.95h,90t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sm_i-7msFFg-8An7jMJ5ngQ!2e0!7i16384!8i8192), going north of Kristiansand, and a couple of [two-digit roads](https://www.google.com/maps/@69.4423175,25.0443757,3a,90y,259.81h,90t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sFvaSuyx1SNMphpL0enMWzw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) in the far north.
NOTE: Regional roads starting with “Fv” do not follow this pattern.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The first digit of road numbers depends on the region, with some exceptions among one- and two-digit roads. A few roads start with 9. Regional "Fv" roads don't follow the pattern.

clues.title: Sign: bilingual with Sámi letters Á and Đ
text: Bilingual signs with **Sámi** can be found in several northern areas in Norway. While the Sámi languages are very different from Norwegian, the best way to recognize them are the letters Á, Đ and the use of several vowels in a row, something which is uncommon in Norwegian.
Note that not all signs in these areas will be bilingual.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some northern signs are in two languages with Sámi, which has letters like Á and Đ and many vowels in a row. Not all signs there are bilingual.

clues.title: Plants: tall bracken fern in the south
text: This species of fern ([Pteridium aquilinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pteridium_aquilinum), also known as bracken) which typically has a fairly tall stem and many wide leaves branching out, is mostly found in the south of Norway. Beware that [other species](https://www.google.com/maps/@69.9525234,19.5216485,3a,22.3y,336.64h,81.92t/data=!3m7!1e1!3m5!1sRk-ap8hooI0Aq3KJMmq_Jg!2e0!5s20180801T000000!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) of ferns can be found further north.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bracken has a fairly tall stem with many wide leaves, and grows mostly in the south. Other ferns grow further north.

clues.title: Trees: spruce in the southern half
text: **Spruces** are mainly found in the southern half of the country, particularly in the southeast and around Trondheim.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Spruces grow mainly in the southern half, especially in the southeast and around Trondheim.

clues.title: Trees: pine on the coast and far inland
text: **Pines** are most common in coastal and far inland areas in the southern half of the country.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Pines are most common on the coast and in far inland areas of the southern half.

clues.title: Trees: oak in the far south
text: **Oaks** are mainly found in the far south of Norway.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Oaks grow mainly in the far south.

clues.title: Trees: maple near southern farmland

clues.title: Landscape: big farmland in three areas
text: Large farmlands are mainly found in **three areas**, the southeast, the area surrounding Trondheim, and south of Stavanger.
_The following clues will explain how to differentiate between the three._

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Large farmland is found in only three areas: the southeast, around Trondheim and south of Stavanger. The next clues tell them apart.

clues.title: Landscape: very flat farmland
text: The largest concentration of farmland is found in the southeast, in the general vicinity of Oslo. The area is **much flatter** than most of the country, and it is common to get a rolling landscape with smooth, round forested hills in the distance. The area southeast of Oslo is particularly flat.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The biggest farmland area, around Oslo, is much flatter than most of the country, with smooth round forested hills in the distance. The area southeast of Oslo is the flattest.

clues.title: Landscape: very hilly farmland, steep and uneven
text: The farmlands surrounding Trondheim are generally **very hilly**, and the hills are typically both steeper and more uneven than in the southeast.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Farmland around Trondheim is very hilly, with hills steeper and more uneven than in the southeast.

clues.title: Landscape: vast grassy fields, round rock walls
text: Similarly to the southeast, the farmland south of Stavanger is flatter than most of the country. However, the fields look more **vast** and open, and it is very common to see **rock walls** made of large, round rocks. Furthermore, rather than crops, most fields will only contain grass.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Farmland south of Stavanger is flat, with vast open fields of grass rather than crops, and walls built from large round rocks.

clues.title: Landscape: deep fjords, tall mountains
text: While fjords can be found along most of the Norwegian coast, **deep fjords** surrounded by **tall mountains** are most common between Bergen and Trondheim.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Deep fjords with tall mountains around them are most common between Bergen and Trondheim.

clues.title: Landscape: sharp rocky peaks, few trees
text: Distinct, **sharp, rocky** mountains with few trees can be seen on the Lofoten Archipelago.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Sharp, rocky mountains with few trees are typical of the Lofoten islands.

clues.title: Landscape: rolling land, tiny birches
text: The northeast of Norway can typically be recognized by a somewhat **rolling landscape**, rather than tall mountains, and vegetation mainly consisting of very **small birches** combined with patched grass.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The northeast has rolling land instead of tall mountains, with very small birches and patchy grass.

clues.title: Vegetation: barren highland, no trees or bushes

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Barren highlands with no trees or bushes, often with rocky mountains by the road, are mostly in the southwest.

clues.title: Landscape: bare rock with small coastal pines

clues.summary: Exposed rock, often dotted with small coastal pines and bushes, is mainly on the south coast.

clues.title: Vegetation: coastal grassland

clues.summary: Coastal grassland with hardly any other plants and low, distant mountains is found on coastal roads in the far north.

clues.summary: Near the Russian border the road looks humid and green with very overcast, sometimes foggy coverage. Trees are fairly low, mostly thin birches and pines.

clues.title: Snow pole: green plastic

clues.title: Snow pole: big wooden sticks
text: **Big wooden sticks** are found on roads that are covered with snow almost the entire year. So far, they've been spotted on the road that runs north of Hardangervidda National Park, on the road west of Jotunheimen and southwest of Valdres Natur-og kulturpark.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Big wooden sticks mark roads that stay snowy almost all year, such as north of Hardangervidda, west of Jotunheimen and southwest of Valdres.

clues.summary: A skinny road with about 1 metre of thick snow beside it and no trees. This is the road between Aadneram and Nomeland.

clues.title: Road: flat, tabletop hill, short scrub
text: The 82 on the island of Andoya, which is part of the Lofoten archipelago, is **flat** apart from **one tabletop looking hill**. In generall, the hills on this road are quite unique and recognizable. You will find **short scrubs** along the road. Often, you will be able to see **water**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A flat road with one hill shaped like a table, short scrub along the road and often water in view, on an island in the far north.

clues.title: Road: very green, big treeless mountains
text: This road is **very green** and usually features **big mountains with no trees**. Right on the Swedish border you will find parts without trees.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A very green road with big mountains that have no trees. Right at the Swedish border there are parts without trees.

clues.title: Road: huge mountains, skinny, bridges
text: This road features **huge mountains**. It is a **skinny road** that has **water to the east**. Lots of sections have **bridges** or **open tunnels**. You will frequently find **fireweed** on the sides of the road. The vegetation on this road has a **yellowish tone**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A skinny road with huge mountains, water to the east, many bridges and open tunnels, fireweed along the sides and yellowish vegetation.

clues.title: Road: valley with treeless mountain range
text: This road **runs through a valley**. You can see a **big mountain range along the road**, with **no trees on the mountain**. Some sections are **very green**, and some section feature **fireweed**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A road through a valley with a big mountain range without trees alongside, some very green parts and some with fireweed.

clues.title: Road: very windy and skinny with 28 hairpins
text: Lysevegen is a **very windy and skinny road** with 28 180° turns down the mountain. Notably, there are **big power lines** visible. You can see **huge mountains** in the distance. The coverage is **very cloudy**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A very windy, skinny road with 28 hairpin turns down a mountain. Big power lines, huge mountains in the distance and very cloudy coverage.

clues.title: Road: no trees, small white rocks
text: This famous road can be identified by the **lack of trees** and the **small white rocks**. The visibility in the coverage is somewhat low. Some sections are very flat, while others can have small hills and lakes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A famous road with no trees and small white rocks, with fairly low visibility. Some parts are flat, others have small hills and lakes.

clues.title: Road: dark-rock bridges, water on both sides
text: This road uses **dark rocks** as bridges. You will see **water on both sides of the road**. The coverage features **dark clouds**.
The road includes the famous Storseisundet bridge.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A road using dark rocks as bridges, with water on both sides and dark clouds. It includes a famous bridge.

clues.title: Coverage: flat island, Gen 2, lots of boats
text: This island has only **Gen 2** coverage. You will see **lots of boats everywhere**. The landscape is **flat** and **islandish** (duh).

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A flat island with only old Gen 2 coverage and lots of boats everywhere.

clues.title: Road: very steep, windy, dark rock with moss
text: Trollstigen leads down a **huge mountain**, and is surrounded by such. The road is **very steep and windy**. The rock is **very dark** and has **green moss** on it. Some sections are cut into the rock, with waterfalls appearing.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: A road down a huge mountain, very steep and windy, with very dark rock and green moss. Some parts are cut into the rock, with waterfalls.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
